title: Κυκλώπων γαῖα
titleEn: The Land of the Cyclopes — Odyssey 9.105–192
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Odysseus, still telling his story at the court of the Phaeacians, sails on from the Lotus-eaters, grieved at the loss of companions, and comes to the land of the Cyclopes, a lawless people who plant nothing and hold no assemblies. He describes an unpeopled island lying off their coast, thick with wild goats and rich in soil, with a harbour that needs no anchor and a spring at its head, and he says that the Cyclopes, with no ships and no shipwrights, have never made use of it. His ships come in there by night under a god's guidance, through mist and without a moon, and the crews spend a day hunting goats and feasting. Next morning he gathers his men, tells them to wait, and sets out with his own ship to learn whether the people across the water are savage or hospitable. Reaching the mainland, he finds a high cave roofed with laurel, its yard walled with stone and trees, and learns of the monstrous man who lives there alone.

sentences.t: ἔνθεν δὲ προτέρω πλέομεν ἀκαχήμενοι ἦτορ·
sentences.tr: enthen de proterō pleomen akachēmenoi ētor·
sentences.l: From there farther we sailed, grieved in heart;
sentences.i: From there we sailed on, grieved at heart.
sentences.n: ἔνθεν 'from there' has the suffix -θεν of place-from, and προτέρω is 'farther on'. πλέομεν is 'we were sailing'. ἀκαχήμενοι ἦτορ is 'grieved in heart', a perfect participle of ἀχέω with ἦτορ 'heart' as an accusative of respect; the same words closed a line of the previous part, and are translated the same. The line ends with a raised dot: the sentence is complete here, and the Cyclopes' land is the next stop.

sentences.t:
Κυκλώπων δ’ ἐς γαῖαν ὑπερφιάλων ἀθεμίστων
ἱκόμεθ’, οἵ ῥα θεοῖσι πεποιθότες ἀθανάτοισιν
οὔτε φυτεύουσιν χερσὶν φυτὸν οὔτ’ ἀρόωσιν,
sentences.tr:
Kyklōpōn d’ es gaian hyperphialōn athemistōn
hikometh’, hoi rha theoisi pepoithotes athanatoisin
oute phyteuousin chersin phyton out’ aroōsin,
sentences.l:
And to the land of the Cyclopes, overweening, lawless,
we came, who, to the gods trusting, the immortal ones,
neither plant with their hands a plant nor plough,
sentences.i: We came to the land of the Cyclopes, an overweening and lawless people, who, trusting in the immortal gods, neither set out plants with their hands nor plough,
sentences.n: Κυκλώπων and the adjectives ὑπερφιάλων ἀθεμίστων are genitive plurals, 'of the Cyclopes, overweening, lawless'; ἱκόμεθ’ is 'we came', an aorist with no augment (Homer's past tenses often drop the ἐ-). ὑπερφίαλος is 'overweening' (its origin is not certain), and ἀθέμιστος is 'lawless', from θέμις, the custom and right that the next lines say they lack. οἵ ῥα is 'who': οἵ is here the relative pronoun (nominative plural of ὅς), with the particle ῥα. θεοῖσι ... ἀθανάτοισιν are datives in -οισι(ν), after πεποιθότες 'trusting'. ἀρόωσιν is uncontracted (= ἀροῦσιν).

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ τά γ’ ἄσπαρτα καὶ ἀνήροτα πάντα φύονται,
πυροὶ καὶ κριθαὶ ἠδ’ ἄμπελοι, αἵ τε φέρουσιν
οἶνον ἐριστάφυλον, καί σφιν Διὸς ὄμβρος ἀέξει.
sentences.tr:
alla ta g’ asparta kai anērota panta phyontai,
pyroi kai krithai ēd’ ampeloi, hai te pherousin
oinon eristaphylon, kai sphin Dios ombros aexei.
sentences.l:
but all those, unsown and unploughed, grow,
wheat and barley and vines, which bear
wine of great clusters, and for them the rain of Zeus makes them grow.
sentences.i: but everything grows unsown and unploughed, wheat and barley and vines, which bear wine from great clusters of grapes, and the rain of Zeus makes it grow for the Cyclopes.
sentences.n: τά γε ... πάντα is 'all those things', the crops of the land, and ἄσπαρτα καὶ ἀνήροτα are two words with the negative prefix ἀ-, 'unsown and unploughed'; φύονται 'grow' is their verb. πυροί is 'wheat' and κριθαί 'barley'. αἵ τε is 'which', with the epic τε that marks a general truth. ἐριστάφυλον is built from ἐρι-, an intensive prefix, and σταφυλή 'bunch of grapes', hence 'of great clusters'. σφιν is 'for them', and Διὸς ὄμβρος 'the rain of Zeus' is how Homer speaks of rain; ἀέξει is 'makes grow'. The line is metrically irregular as transmitted: the short last syllable of ἄσπαρτα must be lengthened in the third foot, and καὶ shortened before the vowel of ἀνήροτα.

sentences.t:
τοῖσιν δ’ οὔτ’ ἀγοραὶ βουληφόροι οὔτε θέμιστες,
ἀλλ’ οἵ γ’ ὑψηλῶν ὀρέων ναίουσι κάρηνα
ἐν σπέσσι γλαφυροῖσι, θεμιστεύει δὲ ἕκαστος
παίδων ἠδ’ ἀλόχων, οὐδ’ ἀλλήλων ἀλέγουσιν.
sentences.tr:
toisin d’ out’ agorai boulēphoroi oute themistes,
all’ hoi g’ hypsēlōn oreōn naiousi karēna
en spessi glaphyroisi, themisteuei de hekastos
paidōn ēd’ alochōn, oud’ allēlōn alegousin.
sentences.l:
And for them there are neither assemblies that bear counsel nor rules of right,
but they on the peaks of high mountains dwell
in hollow caves, and each one lays down the law
for his children and wives, and they take no heed of one another.
sentences.i: They have neither assemblies to deliberate in nor rules of right, but live on the peaks of high mountains in hollow caves, and each one lays down the law for his children and wives, and they pay no heed to one another.
sentences.n: τοῖσιν is 'for them', a pronoun in the dative in -οισιν, and the first clause has no verb: 'there are' has to be supplied for οὔτε ... οὔτε. ἀγοραὶ βουληφόροι are 'assemblies that bear counsel' (βουλή 'counsel' + φέρω), and θέμιστες are the rulings and customs that belong to right order, the same word-family as ἀθέμιστος in line 106. ναίουσι κάρηνα is 'dwell on the heads', that is on the peaks; ὀρέων is the uncontracted genitive of ὄρος. σπέσσι γλαφυροῖσι is a dative plural in -εσσι(ν), from σπέος 'cave'. θεμιστεύει 'lays down the law' governs the genitives παίδων ἠδ’ ἀλόχων, and ἀλέγουσιν 'care for, heed' takes ἀλλήλων.

sentences.t:
νῆσος ἔπειτα λάχεια παρὲκ λιμένος τετάνυσται,
γαίης Κυκλώπων οὔτε σχεδὸν οὔτ’ ἀποτηλοῦ,
ὑλήεσσ’·
sentences.tr:
nēsos epeita lacheia parek limenos tetanystai,
gaiēs Kyklōpōn oute schedon out’ apotēlou,
hylēess’·
sentences.i: Then, outside the harbour, there stretches a low-lying island, neither near to the land of the Cyclopes nor far from it, and wooded;
sentences.n: The scene turns to an island that is not the Cyclopes' own land: γαίης Κυκλώπων 'of the land of the Cyclopes' is the genitive that σχεδόν 'near' and ἀποτηλοῦ 'far away' take, as adverbs of place. λάχεια is of uncertain meaning; 'low-lying, level' is the usual guess, and ὑλήεσσ’ (elided ὑλήεσσα, 'wooded') states separately that the island is wooded. παρὲκ λιμένος is 'outside the harbour', and τετάνυσται is a perfect passive of τανύω, 'has been stretched out', that is 'lies stretched'.

sentences.t:
ἐν δ’ αἶγες ἀπειρέσιαι γεγάασιν
ἄγριαι·
sentences.tr:
en d’ aiges apeiresiai gegaasin
agriai·
sentences.l:
and on it goats past counting have come to be,
wild;
sentences.i: and on it countless wild goats have come to be;
sentences.n: ἐν δ’ is 'and in it, on it': ἐν is an adverb, and goes closely with γεγάασιν. ἀπειρέσιαι 'countless' goes with αἶγες 'goats' and is related to ἀπείρων 'boundless'. γεγάασιν is the epic third plural perfect of γίγνομαι (= Attic γεγόνασιν), 'have come to be', so 'are there'. The goats are ἄγριαι 'wild', which the hunt at lines 154–158 will use.

sentences.t:
οὐ μὲν γὰρ πάτος ἀνθρώπων ἀπερύκει,
οὐδέ μιν εἰσοιχνεῦσι κυνηγέται, οἵ τε καθ’ ὕλην
ἄλγεα πάσχουσιν κορυφὰς ὀρέων ἐφέποντες.
sentences.tr:
ou men gar patos anthrōpōn aperykei,
oude min eisoichneusi kynēgetai, hoi te kath’ hylēn
algea paschousin koryphas oreōn ephepontes.
sentences.i: for no track trodden by men keeps them away, nor do hunters come into it, the kind who suffer pains in the woods as they range over mountain peaks.
sentences.n: πάτος is 'tread, trodden way' and ἀπερύκει 'keeps away': the goats are undisturbed. μιν is 'it', the island, and εἰσοιχνεῦσι is 'go into, enter'. οἵ τε is 'who', with the epic τε that gives what hunters as a class do. καθ’ ὕλην is 'through the woods'. ἄλγεα is the object of πάσχουσιν 'suffer pains', and κορυφάς 'peaks' is the object of ἐφέποντες 'going over'; ὀρέων is uncontracted.

sentences.t:
οὔτ’ ἄρα ποίμνῃσιν καταΐσχεται οὔτ’ ἀρότοισιν,
ἀλλ’ ἥ γ’ ἄσπαρτος καὶ ἀνήροτος ἤματα πάντα
ἀνδρῶν χηρεύει, βόσκει δέ τε μηκάδας αἶγας.
sentences.tr:
out’ ara poimnēisin kataïschetai out’ arotoisin,
all’ hē g’ aspartos kai anērotos ēmata panta
andrōn chēreuei, boskei de te mēkadas aigas.
sentences.l:
Nor by flocks is it occupied nor by ploughings,
but it, unsown and unploughed all its days,
is widowed of men, and feeds the bleating goats.
sentences.i: It is taken up neither by flocks nor by ploughing, but lies unsown and unploughed all its days, empty of men, and it feeds the bleating goats.
sentences.n: καταΐσχεται is 'is held, is occupied' (καταΐσχω is a poetic form of κατίσχω = κατέχω, here in the passive), with the datives ποίμνῃσιν 'by flocks', a dative in -ῃσιν, and ἀρότοισιν 'by ploughings'. ἥ γε is 'it', the island (νῆσος is feminine). ἄσπαρτος καὶ ἀνήροτος repeats the pair of line 109, in the singular, and ἤματα πάντα is 'all the days', that is always. χηρεύει 'is widowed of, is bereft of' takes the genitive ἀνδρῶν. In βόσκει δέ τε the τε is the epic particle; μηκάδας 'bleating' is from μηκάομαι 'to bleat'.

sentences.t: οὐ γὰρ Κυκλώπεσσι νέες πάρα μιλτοπάρῃοι,
sentences.tr: ou gar Kyklōpessi nees para miltoparēioi,
sentences.l: For to the Cyclopes there are no ships, red-cheeked,
sentences.i: For the Cyclopes have no red-cheeked ships,
sentences.n: Κυκλώπεσσι is a dative plural in -εσσι, and πάρα stands for πάρεισι(ν) 'are at hand' (the accent thrown back), so 'the Cyclopes have no ships'. νέες is an epic by-form of νῆες, the plural of ναῦς. μιλτοπάρῃοι 'red-cheeked' is built on μίλτος 'red ochre' and παρῃά 'cheek'; a ship's cheeks are the sides of its bow, painted red. The sentence is long and runs on for five lines, so it is broken here at the comma.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄνδρες νηῶν ἔνι τέκτονες, οἵ κε κάμοιεν
νῆας ἐυσσέλμους, αἵ κεν τελέοιεν ἕκαστα
ἄστε’ ἐπ’ ἀνθρώπων ἱκνεύμεναι, οἷά τε πολλὰ
ἄνδρες ἐπ’ ἀλλήλους νηυσὶν περόωσι θάλασσαν·
sentences.tr:
oud’ andres nēōn eni tektones, hoi ke kamoien
nēas eysselmous, hai ken teleoien hekasta
aste’ ep’ anthrōpōn hikneumenai, hoia te polla
andres ep’ allēlous nēusin peroōsi thalassan·
sentences.l:
nor men among them, shipwrights, who could build
well-benched ships, which would accomplish everything,
reaching the cities of men, such things as often
men to one another in ships cross the sea;
sentences.i: nor do they have shipwrights among them, who could build well-benched ships to serve every purpose by reaching the cities of men, as men so often cross the sea in ships to visit one another;
sentences.n: ἔνι is here ἔνεισι(ν) 'there are among them', and τέκτονες νηῶν 'builders of ships' are the men who are missing. οἵ κε κάμοιεν is 'who could build', the optative with κε (= ἄν), and νῆας ἐυσσέλμους is 'well-benched ships' (σέλμα is a ship's bench or thwart). αἵ κεν τελέοιεν ἕκαστα is 'which would bring each thing to its end', that is do all that ships are for. ἄστε’ is elided ἄστεα 'cities', ἐπ’ ἀνθρώπων is 'among men', and ἱκνεύμεναι is an infinitive in -μεναι, 'to reach'. οἷά τε is 'such as', with the epic τε. περόωσι is uncontracted (= περῶσι) and takes θάλασσαν, 'cross the sea'.

sentences.t: οἵ κέ σφιν καὶ νῆσον ἐυκτιμένην ἐκάμοντο.
sentences.tr: hoi ke sphin kai nēson eyktimenēn ekamonto.
sentences.l: Those would have made for them also the island well-built.
sentences.i: Such men would also have made the island a well-settled place for them.
sentences.n: οἵ κε ... ἐκάμοντο is a past 'would have' statement (κε with a past tense) whose condition is left unstated: had such men been there. ἐκάμοντο is the middle aorist of κάμνω 'work at, build', and σφιν is 'for them', the Cyclopes. ἐυκτιμένην is built on κτίζω 'found, settle': of a town it is 'well-built', of an island, as here, 'well-settled'; the layer that follows the Greek word by word keeps 'well-built'.

sentences.t: οὐ μὲν γάρ τι κακή γε, φέροι δέ κεν ὥρια πάντα·
sentences.tr: ou men gar ti kakē ge, pheroi de ken hōria panta·
sentences.l: For it is by no means a bad one, and it would bear all things in season;
sentences.i: For it is by no means a poor island, and it would bear everything in its season;
sentences.n: οὐ μὲν γάρ τι is 'for not at all', and κακή γε picks up νῆσος: the double denial (litotes) means that the island is good. φέροι δέ κεν is an optative with κε, 'it would bear'; ὥρια πάντα are 'all things of their season', from ὥρα 'season'.

sentences.t:
ἐν μὲν γὰρ λειμῶνες ἁλὸς πολιοῖο παρ’ ὄχθας
ὑδρηλοὶ μαλακοί·
sentences.tr:
en men gar leimōnes halos polioio par’ ochthas
hydrēloi malakoi·
sentences.l:
For in it are meadows along the shores of the grey sea,
well-watered, soft;
sentences.i: For it has meadows along the shores of the grey sea, well-watered and soft;
sentences.n: ἐν μὲν γάρ begins a list of what the island has, and the ἐν is again 'in it', with no verb: the list is taken up by ἐν δ’ in lines 134 and 136. λειμῶνες are 'meadows'. ἁλὸς πολιοῖο is 'of the grey sea', the salt water, with the genitive in -οιο; παρ’ ὄχθας is 'along the banks, the shores'. ὑδρηλοί is 'well-watered', and μαλακοί 'soft'.

sentences.t: μάλα κ’ ἄφθιτοι ἄμπελοι εἶεν.
sentences.tr: mala k’ aphthitoi ampeloi eien.
sentences.l: very much unfailing the vines would be.
sentences.i: There the vines would never fail.
sentences.n: μάλα κ’ is μάλα κε, 'very much, indeed'. ἄφθιτοι is 'unfailing' (ἀ- + φθίνω 'perish, wither'), and εἶεν is the optative of εἰμί, the 'would be' that carries the whole description: what the island might be if it were worked.

sentences.t: ἐν δ’ ἄροσις λείη·
sentences.tr: en d’ arosis leiē·
sentences.l: and in it, ploughland, smooth;
sentences.i: and it has smooth ploughland;
sentences.n: ἄροσις is 'ploughing, ploughland', and λείη is 'smooth, level'. This is the second of the ἐν-clauses that list what the island has.

sentences.t:
μάλα κεν βαθὺ λήιον αἰεὶ
εἰς ὥρας ἀμῷεν, ἐπεὶ μάλα πῖαρ ὑπ’ οὖδας.
sentences.tr:
mala ken bathy lēion aiei
eis hōras amōien, epei mala piar hyp’ oudas.
sentences.l:
very much a deep crop, always,
in season they would reap, since very rich is it beneath the ground.
sentences.i: Men would always reap a very deep crop there in season, since the soil beneath is very rich.
sentences.n: ἀμῷεν is the optative of ἀμάω 'reap', with κε, 'they would reap', the doer being an indefinite 'they'; βαθὺ λήιον is 'a deep standing crop', and αἰεί is the epic form of ἀεί 'always'. εἰς ὥρας is 'at the seasons, in season'. ἐπεὶ μάλα πῖαρ ὑπ’ οὖδας is 'since it is very rich under the ground', with no verb: πῖαρ, 'fat, rich', is a neuter noun used as a predicate, and οὖδας is 'ground'.

sentences.t:
ἐν δὲ λιμὴν ἐύορμος, ἵν’ οὐ χρεὼ πείσματός ἐστιν,
οὔτ’ εὐνὰς βαλέειν οὔτε πρυμνήσι’ ἀνάψαι,
ἀλλ’ ἐπικέλσαντας μεῖναι χρόνον εἰς ὅ κε ναυτέων
θυμὸς ἐποτρύνῃ καὶ ἐπιπνεύσωσιν ἀῆται.
sentences.tr:
en de limēn eyormos, hin’ ou chreō peismatos estin,
out’ eunas baleein oute prymnēsi’ anapsai,
all’ epikelsantas meinai chronon eis ho ke nauteōn
thymos epotrynēi kai epipneusōsin aētai.
sentences.l:
and in it a harbour good for mooring, where there is no need of a cable,
either to throw out anchor-stones or to fasten stern-cables,
but, having run ashore, to wait a while, until the sailors’
heart urges them on and the breezes blow.
sentences.i: It has a harbour good for mooring, where there is no need of a cable, neither to throw out anchor-stones nor to make fast stern-cables, but men may run ashore and wait until the sailors’ heart urges them on and the breezes blow.
sentences.n: ἵν’ is 'where'. οὐ χρεὼ ... ἐστιν is 'there is no need', and χρεώ takes the genitive πείσματος 'of a cable' and three infinitives: βαλέειν (uncontracted) 'to throw', ἀνάψαι 'to fasten' and, after ἀλλά, μεῖναι 'to wait'. εὐναί are the anchor-stones ('beds', let down to hold a ship), and πρυμνήσια the stern-cables made fast ashore. ἐύορμος is 'good for mooring'. ἐπικέλσαντας is 'having run ashore' (the ships understood), and χρόνον 'for a time' goes with μεῖναι. εἰς ὅ κε ... ἐποτρύνῃ is 'until ... urges on', with the subjunctive and κε, and θυμός is 'heart'. ναυτέων is an uncontracted genitive plural, and ἀῆται 'breezes' (ἀήτης) is the subject of ἐπιπνεύσωσιν 'blow upon'.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπὶ κρατὸς λιμένος ῥέει ἀγλαὸν ὕδωρ,
κρήνη ὑπὸ σπείους·
sentences.tr:
autar epi kratos limenos rheei aglaon hydōr,
krēnē hypo speious·
sentences.l:
But at the head of the harbour flows splendid water,
a spring beneath a cave;
sentences.i: At the head of the harbour splendid water flows, a spring beneath a cave;
sentences.n: ἐπὶ κρατὸς λιμένος is 'at the head of the harbour', its inner end, with the genitive. ἀγλαόν is 'splendid': the word is a general one of brightness and show, and it is kept as 'splendid' even of water. κρήνη ὑπὸ σπείους is 'a spring under a cave', and σπείους is the Homeric genitive of σπέος.

sentences.t: περὶ δ’ αἴγειροι πεφύασιν.
sentences.tr: peri d’ aigeiroi pephyasin.
sentences.l: and around, poplars have grown.
sentences.i: and poplars grow all round it.
sentences.n: περί is an adverb, 'around'. αἴγειροι are poplars, and πεφύασιν is the perfect of φύω, 'have grown, stand grown', that is are there now.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα κατεπλέομεν, καί τις θεὸς ἡγεμόνευεν
νύκτα δι’ ὀρφναίην, οὐδὲ προυφαίνετ’ ἰδέσθαι·
sentences.tr:
entha katepleomen, kai tis theos hēgemoneuen
nykta di’ orphnaiēn, oude prouphainet’ idesthai·
sentences.l:
There we sailed in, and some god was leading us
through the murky night, nor did it show forth to be seen;
sentences.i: We sailed in there, and some god was our guide through the murky night, and the island did not show itself to be seen;
sentences.n: κατεπλέομεν is 'we were sailing down to land', an imperfect of κατα-πλέω. καί τις θεὸς ἡγεμόνευεν is 'and some god was leading the way', and Odysseus does not say which god. νύκτα δι’ ὀρφναίην is 'through the murky night' (ὀρφναῖος 'murky'), with διά and the accusative. προυφαίνετ’ is προφαίνετο 'was showing forth', with ἰδέσθαι 'to be seen' (aorist infinitive of ὁράω, middle form); the subject, the island, is not named, and the next unit gives the reason.

sentences.t:
ἀὴρ γὰρ περὶ νηυσὶ βαθεῖ’ ἦν, οὐδὲ σελήνη
οὐρανόθεν προύφαινε, κατείχετο δὲ νεφέεσσιν.
sentences.tr:
aēr gar peri nēusi bathei’ ēn, oude selēnē
ouranothen prouphaine, kateicheto de nepheessin.
sentences.l:
For a mist, deep, about the ships there was, nor did the moon
shine forth from heaven, but was held in by clouds.
sentences.i: For a deep mist lay about the ships, and the moon did not shine out from the sky, but was held in by clouds.
sentences.n: ἀήρ here is 'mist, murk', not the upper air, and it is feminine, as βαθεῖ’ (elided βαθεῖα 'deep, thick') shows; and νηυσί is the dative plural of ναῦς, after περί 'around'. οὐρανόθεν is 'from heaven', with the suffix -θεν. κατείχετο is an imperfect passive, 'was held down, was kept in', and the dative νεφέεσσιν 'by clouds' is in -εσσι.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ οὔ τις τὴν νῆσον ἐσέδρακεν ὀφθαλμοῖσιν,
οὔτ’ οὖν κύματα μακρὰ κυλινδόμενα προτὶ χέρσον
εἰσίδομεν, πρὶν νῆας ἐυσσέλμους ἐπικέλσαι.
sentences.tr:
enth’ ou tis tēn nēson esedraken ophthalmoisin,
out’ oun kymata makra kylindomena proti cherson
eisidomen, prin nēas eysselmous epikelsai.
sentences.l:
Then no one saw the island with his eyes,
nor indeed the long waves rolling toward the dry land
did we see, before we ran the well-benched ships ashore.
sentences.i: Then no one caught sight of the island with his own eyes, nor did we see the long waves rolling toward the shore, until we had run our well-benched ships ashore.
sentences.n: ἐσέδρακεν is an aorist of δέρκομαι 'see, look', from the root δρακ-, with the preverb ἐς- 'at', and ὀφθαλμοῖσιν is a dative plural in -οισιν, 'with eyes'. The subject shifts from οὔ τις 'no one' to 'we' in εἰσίδομεν 'we saw' (aorist without augment). οὔτ’ οὖν is 'nor indeed', and προτὶ χέρσον is 'toward the dry land' (προτί = πρός). πρὶν ... ἐπικέλσαι is πρίν with an infinitive, 'before running ashore'. The sentence says that the whole approach was made blind.

sentences.t:
κελσάσῃσι δὲ νηυσὶ καθείλομεν ἱστία πάντα,
ἐκ δὲ καὶ αὐτοὶ βῆμεν ἐπὶ ῥηγμῖνι θαλάσσης·
sentences.tr:
kelsasēisi de nēusi katheilomen histia panta,
ek de kai autoi bēmen epi rhēgmini thalassēs·
sentences.l:
And the ships having run ashore, we lowered all the sails,
and out too we ourselves stepped upon the surf-line of the sea;
sentences.i: When the ships had run ashore, we lowered all the sails, and we ourselves too stepped out onto the shore where the sea breaks;
sentences.n: κελσάσῃσι νηυσί is 'the ships having run aground', a feminine dative plural participle of κέλλω, in -ῃσι. καθείλομεν is 'we took down' (καθαιρέω). ἐκ δὲ ... βῆμεν is tmesis, a preverb standing apart from its verb: 'we stepped out'; βῆμεν is an epic aorist of βαίνω with no augment. ῥηγμῖνι is the surf, the breaking edge of the water (from ῥήγνυμι 'break'), and ἐπί takes the dative.

sentences.t: ἔνθα δ’ ἀποβρίξαντες ἐμείναμεν Ἠῶ δῖαν.
sentences.tr: entha d’ apobrixantes emeinamen Ēō dian.
sentences.l: And there, having slept, we waited for heavenly Dawn.
sentences.i: There we slept and waited for heavenly Dawn.
sentences.n: Ἠῶ is the accusative of Ἠώς 'Dawn', a goddess, and δῖαν is the feminine of δῖος, kept as 'heavenly' wherever it stands. ἀποβρίξαντες is a participle of a rare verb, ἀποβρίζω, taken from the context to mean 'having slept' (the exact sense is not certain). ἐμείναμεν is 'we waited for', with the accusative.

sentences.t:
ἦμος δ’ ἠριγένεια φάνη ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠώς,
νῆσον θαυμάζοντες ἐδινεόμεσθα κατ’ αὐτήν.
sentences.tr:
ēmos d’ ērigeneia phanē rhododaktylos Ēōs,
nēson thaumazontes edineomestha kat’ autēn.
sentences.l:
When early-born appeared, rose-fingered Dawn,
wondering at the island, we roamed over it.
sentences.i: When early-born Dawn appeared, rose-fingered, we roamed over the island, marvelling at it.
sentences.n: The dawn line: ἦμος is 'when', ἠριγένεια is 'early-born' and ῥοδοδάκτυλος 'rose-fingered'; φάνη is an aorist passive with no augment, 'appeared'. The same line comes again at 170, and it is translated the same each time. νῆσον θαυμάζοντες is 'wondering at the island', and ἐδινεόμεσθα is 'we were roaming about', an uncontracted imperfect with the epic ending -όμεσθα (= -όμεθα), from δινέω 'whirl, wander'; κατ’ αὐτήν is 'over it'.

sentences.t:
ὦρσαν δὲ νύμφαι, κοῦραι Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο,
αἶγας ὀρεσκῴους, ἵνα δειπνήσειαν ἑταῖροι.
sentences.tr:
ōrsan de nymphai, kourai Dios aigiochoio,
aigas oreskōious, hina deipnēseian hetairoi.
sentences.l:
And the nymphs, daughters of aegis-bearing Zeus, roused
goats of the mountain-bed, so that the companions might dine.
sentences.i: The nymphs, daughters of aegis-bearing Zeus, roused mountain goats so that my companions might have a meal.
sentences.n: ὦρσαν is the aorist of ὄρνυμι 'rouse, stir up', and νύμφαι are nymphs, the spirits of the wild. κοῦραι Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο is 'daughters of aegis-bearing Zeus'; the sense of αἰγίοχος is disputed ('holding the aegis', or something to do with goats), and 'aegis-bearing' follows the usual reading. ὀρεσκῴους is usually explained as 'that lie on the mountains', from ὄρος 'mountain' and a second element from κοῖτος 'bed'. ἵνα δειπνήσειαν is 'so that they might dine', a purpose clause with the optative, and ἑταῖροι are 'the companions', mine.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα καμπύλα τόξα καὶ αἰγανέας δολιχαύλους
εἱλόμεθ’ ἐκ νηῶν, διὰ δὲ τρίχα κοσμηθέντες
βάλλομεν·
sentences.tr:
autika kampyla toxa kai aiganeas dolichaulous
heilometh’ ek nēōn, dia de tricha kosmēthentes
ballomen·
sentences.i: At once we took our curved bows and long-socketed javelins from the ships, and, arranged in three companies, we shot;
sentences.n: αἰγανέας are light throwing-spears, javelins, and δολιχαύλους is 'long-socketed', from δολιχός 'long' and αὐλός 'tube, socket'; the second element is uncertain. εἱλόμεθ’ is εἱλόμεθα, an aorist middle of αἱρέω, 'we took for ourselves'. διὰ ... τρίχα is 'in three parts', and κοσμηθέντες 'arranged, drawn up': the crews are divided into three companies. βάλλομεν is an imperfect, 'we were shooting'. The rest of line 158, in the next unit, gives the result.

sentences.t: αἶψα δ’ ἔδωκε θεὸς μενοεικέα θήρην.
sentences.tr: aipsa d’ edōke theos menoeikea thērēn.
sentences.l: and quickly a god gave a hunt to the heart’s liking.
sentences.i: and quickly a god gave us a catch to our heart’s liking.
sentences.n: αἶψα is 'quickly', and ἔδωκε 'gave'; θεός is again an unnamed god, as at line 142. μενοεικέα is 'to the liking of the μένος' (μένος 'spirit, desire' + a second element from εἴκω 'yield' or ἔοικα 'be fitting'), that is 'as much as the heart wishes'. θήρη is 'hunt', and here 'game caught'.

sentences.t:
νῆες μέν μοι ἕποντο δυώδεκα, ἐς δὲ ἑκάστην
ἐννέα λάγχανον αἶγες·
sentences.tr:
nēes men moi heponto dyōdeka, es de hekastēn
ennea lanchanon aiges·
sentences.l:
Ships, for me, followed, twelve, and to each
nine goats fell by lot;
sentences.i: Twelve ships followed me, and nine goats fell by lot to each;
sentences.n: νῆες μέν μοι ἕποντο is 'ships followed me', with ἕποντο an imperfect of ἕπομαι 'follow', without the augment; δυώδεκα is 'twelve'. ἐς δὲ ἑκάστην is 'to each one', with ἐς = εἰς. λάγχανον is an imperfect of λαγχάνω 'obtain by lot', and it agrees with αἶγες 'goats': nine goats were allotted to each crew.

sentences.t: ἐμοὶ δὲ δέκ’ ἔξελον οἴῳ.
sentences.tr: emoi de dek’ exelon oiōi.
sentences.l: but for me, ten they picked out, for me alone.
sentences.i: but for me alone they picked out ten.
sentences.n: ἐμοὶ ... οἴῳ is 'for me alone', a dative with οἶος 'alone'. ἔξελον is 'they picked out' (aorist of ἐξαιρέω, with no augment); the subject, his companions, is left out, and the ten goats are the leader's extra share.

sentences.t:
ὣς τότε μὲν πρόπαν ἦμαρ ἐς ἠέλιον καταδύντα
ἥμεθα δαινύμενοι κρέα τ’ ἄσπετα καὶ μέθυ ἡδύ·
sentences.tr:
hōs tote men propan ēmar es ēelion katadynta
hēmetha dainymenoi krea t’ aspeta kai methy hēdy·
sentences.l:
So then for the whole day, until the sun going down,
we sat feasting on boundless meat and sweet wine;
sentences.i: So for that whole day, until the sun went down, we sat feasting on boundless meat and sweet wine;
sentences.n: ὣς is 'so, thus', and τότε μέν 'then, on the one hand'. πρόπαν ἦμαρ is 'the whole day', an accusative of duration, and ἐς ἠέλιον καταδύντα 'until the sun sinking'. ἥμεθα is 'we sat' (from ἧμαι), and δαινύμενοι is 'feasting'. κρέα is 'meat', a neuter plural, and ἄσπετα is 'boundless', literally 'not to be told', that is too great for words. μέθυ is 'wine', and ἡδύ 'sweet'.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ πω νηῶν ἐξέφθιτο οἶνος ἐρυθρός,
ἀλλ’ ἐνέην·
sentences.tr:
ou gar pō nēōn exephthito oinos erythros,
all’ eneēn·
sentences.l:
For not yet from the ships had the wine run out, red,
but there was some in them;
sentences.i: For the red wine had not yet run out on the ships, but there was still some aboard;
sentences.n: οὐ γάρ πω is 'for not yet', and ἐξέφθιτο is an aorist middle of ἐκφθίνω 'perish, be used up', which English renders 'had run out', with the genitive νηῶν 'from the ships'. οἶνος ἐρυθρός is 'red wine'; ἐρυθρός is plain 'red'. ἐνέην is 'there was in them', an uncontracted imperfect of ἔνειμι (= ἐνῆν).

sentences.t:
πολλὸν γὰρ ἐν ἀμφιφορεῦσιν ἕκαστοι
ἠφύσαμεν Κικόνων.
sentences.tr:
pollon gar en amphiphoreusin hekastoi
ēphysamen Kikonōn.
sentences.l:
for much, in amphoras, each of us
had drawn off, of the Cicones.
sentences.i: for each of us had drawn off much of it into jars from the Cicones.
sentences.n: πολλὸν is an epic form of πολύ 'much', an accusative, and ἐν ἀμφιφορεῦσιν is 'in amphoras', two-handled jars, a dative plural. ἕκαστοι is 'each', with the first-person ἠφύσαμεν 'we drew off' (ἀφύσσω 'draw liquid'), so 'each of us'. Κικόνων is a genitive that belongs with πτολίεθρον in the next unit, 'the citadel of the Cicones'; the archive prints a full stop after it, so it closes this unit, and the English here reads it loosely as 'from the Cicones'.

sentences.t: ἱερὸν πτολίεθρον ἑλόντες.
sentences.tr: hieron ptoliethron helontes.
sentences.l: the holy citadel having taken.
sentences.i: when we took their holy citadel.
sentences.n: Κικόνων, the last word of the unit before, is the genitive that goes with this phrase: ἱερὸν πτολίεθρον is 'the holy citadel' of the Cicones, and ἑλόντες is 'having taken' (aorist participle of αἱρέω), agreeing with the 'we' of ἠφύσαμεν. The archive prints a full stop after Κικόνων, so the phrase stands here as a unit of its own. πτολίεθρον is an epic form of 'citadel, town'.

sentences.t:
Κυκλώπων δ’ ἐς γαῖαν ἐλεύσσομεν ἐγγὺς ἐόντων,
καπνόν τ’ αὐτῶν τε φθογγὴν ὀίων τε καὶ αἰγῶν.
sentences.tr:
Kyklōpōn d’ es gaian eleussomen engys eontōn,
kapnon t’ autōn te phthongēn oiōn te kai aigōn.
sentences.l:
And to the land of the Cyclopes we gazed, being near,
and at smoke, and at their voice, and of sheep and of goats.
sentences.i: We looked toward the land of the Cyclopes, who were near, and could make out their smoke and the sound of their voices, and of sheep and goats.
sentences.n: ἐλεύσσομεν is 'we were gazing', with ἐς γαῖαν 'at the land', and Κυκλώπων ... ἐγγὺς ἐόντων is a genitive plural, 'the Cyclopes being near' (ἐόντων is the epic participle of εἰμί, = ὄντων). καπνόν is 'smoke', and φθογγήν 'voice, sound', with αὐτῶν 'their', of the Cyclopes. ὀίων τε καὶ αἰγῶν is 'of sheep and of goats', also depending on φθογγήν, ὀίων being the uncontracted genitive plural of ὄις. The verb 'gaze' stands for sight and hearing both.

sentences.t:
ἦμος δ’ ἠέλιος κατέδυ καὶ ἐπὶ κνέφας ἦλθε,
δὴ τότε κοιμήθημεν ἐπὶ ῥηγμῖνι θαλάσσης.
sentences.tr:
ēmos d’ ēelios katedy kai epi knephas ēlthe,
dē tote koimēthēmen epi rhēgmini thalassēs.
sentences.l:
And when the sun set and darkness came on,
then indeed we lay down to sleep upon the surf-line of the sea.
sentences.i: And when the sun set and darkness came on, then we lay down to sleep on the shore where the sea breaks.
sentences.n: ἦμος δ’ is 'and when', with the aorists κατέδυ 'set' and ἦλθε 'came'; ἐπί is an adverb here, and κνέφας is 'darkness, dusk'. δὴ τότε is 'then indeed', which opens the main clause. κοιμήθημεν is an aorist passive of κοιμάω, 'we were put to sleep', that is 'lay down to sleep'. The second line comes again from earlier in the poem and is translated the same; ῥηγμῖνι θαλάσσης is 'the surf-line of the sea', as at 150.

sentences.t:
ἦμος δ’ ἠριγένεια φάνη ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠώς,
καὶ τότ’ ἐγὼν ἀγορὴν θέμενος μετὰ πᾶσιν ἔειπον·
sentences.tr:
ēmos d’ ērigeneia phanē rhododaktylos Ēōs,
kai tot’ egōn agorēn themenos meta pasin eeipon·
sentences.l:
When early-born appeared, rose-fingered Dawn,
then I, an assembly having set, among all spoke:
sentences.i: When early-born Dawn appeared, rose-fingered, I called an assembly and spoke among them all:
sentences.n: The dawn line of 152 comes again and is translated the same. The main clause begins καὶ τότ’ 'and then', with ἐγών, the epic form of ἐγώ 'I'; ἀγορὴν θέμενος is 'having set an assembly', that is 'having called a meeting', and μετὰ πᾶσιν ἔειπον is 'I spoke among them all', ἔειπον being an aorist (= εἶπον). What follows, to line 176, is a speech inside Odysseus' own telling; it carries single quotation marks, since he is himself speaking.

sentences.t: ἄλλοι μὲν νῦν μίμνετ’, ἐμοὶ ἐρίηρες ἑταῖροι·
sentences.tr: alloi men nyn mimnet’, emoi eriēres hetairoi·
sentences.l: ‘The rest of you, for now, stay, my trusty companions;
sentences.i: ‘The rest of you, my trusty companions, stay here for now;
sentences.n: ἄλλοι μὲν νῦν is 'the others, for now', and μέν looks ahead to the contrast of αὐτὰρ ἐγώ 'but I' in the next unit. μίμνετ’ is an imperative of μίμνω 'stay'. ἐμοὶ ἐρίηρες ἑταῖροι is 'my trusty companions', with ἐμοί a dative of possession, 'to me'; the sense of ἐρίηρες is not fully known, and 'trusty' is the traditional guess.
sentences.mark: Odysseus recalls his speech to the assembly

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ σὺν νηί τ’ ἐμῇ καὶ ἐμοῖς ἑτάροισιν
ἐλθὼν τῶνδ’ ἀνδρῶν πειρήσομαι, οἵ τινές εἰσιν,
ἤ ῥ’ οἵ γ’ ὑβρισταί τε καὶ ἄγριοι οὐδὲ δίκαιοι,
ἦε φιλόξεινοι, καί σφιν νόος ἐστὶ θεουδής.
sentences.tr:
autar egō syn nēi t’ emēi kai emois hetaroisin
elthōn tōnd’ andrōn peirēsomai, hoi tines eisin,
ē rh’ hoi g’ hybristai te kai agrioi oude dikaioi,
ēe philoxeinoi, kai sphin noos esti theoudēs.
sentences.l:
but I, with my ship and with my companions,
going, will make trial of these men, who they are,
whether it is that they are violent and savage and not just,
or guest-loving, and to them the mind is god-fearing.’
sentences.i: but I, with my ship and my companions, will go and make trial of these men, to learn who they are, whether they are violent and savage and unjust, or hospitable, with a god-fearing mind.’
sentences.n: πειρήσομαι is a future middle of πειράω 'try, test', with the genitive τῶνδ’ ἀνδρῶν 'these men'; οἵ τινές εἰσιν is an indirect question, 'who they are'. ἤ ῥ’ ... ἦε is 'whether ... or'. ὑβρισταί is from ὕβρις, 'violent, insolent men', and ἄγριοι is 'savage'; οὐδὲ δίκαιοι is 'nor just'. φιλόξεινοι is 'guest-loving' (φίλος + ξένος), the opposite; σφιν is 'to them', and θεουδής is 'god-fearing' (θεός + δέος 'fear'). ἑτάροισιν is a dative in -οισιν, and the closing mark ends the quoted speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν ἀνὰ νηὸς ἔβην, ἐκέλευσα δ’ ἑταίρους
αὐτούς τ’ ἀμβαίνειν ἀνά τε πρυμνήσια λῦσαι.
sentences.tr:
hōs eipōn ana nēos ebēn, ekeleusa d’ hetairous
autous t’ ambainein ana te prymnēsia lysai.
sentences.l:
So having spoken, up onto the ship I went, and I ordered my companions
themselves to embark and to loose the stern-cables.
sentences.i: So saying, I went up on board and ordered my companions themselves to embark and to cast off the stern-cables.
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών is 'so having spoken', the narrator's words that close the quoted speech. ἀνὰ νηός is ἀνά with the genitive, 'up onto the ship' (νηός is the epic genitive of ναῦς), and ἔβην is an aorist of βαίνω. ἐκέλευσα ... αὐτούς τ’ ἀμβαίνειν is 'I ordered ... themselves to embark' (ἀμβαίνειν = ἀναβαίνειν), where αὐτούς 'themselves' says that they too, not only he, are to board. ἀνά τε ... λῦσαι is tmesis, = ἀναλῦσαι 'to loose', and πρυμνήσια are the stern-cables, as at 137.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ αἶψ’ εἴσβαινον καὶ ἐπὶ κληῖσι καθῖζον,
ἑξῆς δ’ ἑζόμενοι πολιὴν ἅλα τύπτον ἐρετμοῖς.
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ aips’ eisbainon kai epi klēisi kathizon,
hexēs d’ hezomenoi poliēn hala typton eretmois.
sentences.l:
And they quickly went aboard and on the rowing-benches sat down,
and sitting in a row, the grey sea they struck with their oars.
sentences.i: They quickly went aboard and sat down at the oarlocks, and sitting in rows, they struck the grey sea with their oars.
sentences.n: The subject changes to the crew, οἱ δ’ 'and they'. εἴσβαινον is an imperfect, 'were going aboard'. κληῖσι is a dative of κληΐς 'rowing-bench', and καθῖζον is 'they sat down'. ἑξῆς is 'in order, in a row', and ἑζόμενοι is a participle of ἕζομαι 'seat oneself'. πολιὴν ἅλα is 'the grey sea', ἅλς being the salt sea, and ἐρετμοῖς is a dative plural of ἐρετμόν 'oar'. The two lines are a stock description of a crew putting to sea, and they are translated the same each time they come.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ τὸν χῶρον ἀφικόμεθ’ ἐγγὺς ἐόντα,
ἔνθα δ’ ἐπ’ ἐσχατιῇ σπέος εἴδομεν ἄγχι θαλάσσης,
ὑψηλόν, δάφνῃσι κατηρεφές.
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē ton chōron aphikometh’ engys eonta,
entha d’ ep’ eschatiēi speos eidomen anchi thalassēs,
hypsēlon, daphnēisi katērephes.
sentences.l:
But when to the place we came, being near,
there at the edge a cave we saw, near the sea,
high, roofed over with laurels.
sentences.i: But when we reached the place, which was near, we saw at its edge, close by the sea, a cave, high and roofed over with laurels.
sentences.n: ἀφικόμεθ’ is 'we came to' (an aorist middle), with τὸν χῶρον 'that place' and ἐγγὺς ἐόντα agreeing with it, 'being near'. ἐπ’ ἐσχατιῇ is 'at the edge' of the land, and σπέος is 'cave', εἴδομεν 'we saw' (aorist of ὁράω), and ἄγχι 'near'. ὑψηλόν is 'high', and δάφνῃσι, a dative in -ῃσι, is 'with laurels'; κατηρεφές is 'roofed over'. The cave's owner is not yet named.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα δὲ πολλὰ
μῆλ’, ὄιές τε καὶ αἶγες, ἰαύεσκον·
sentences.tr:
entha de polla
mēl’, oies te kai aiges, iaueskon·
sentences.l:
And there many
flocks, sheep and goats, used to sleep;
sentences.i: Many flocks of sheep and goats used to sleep there;
sentences.n: ἔνθα here is 'there', in the cave. μῆλα is a neuter plural for small livestock, 'flocks', and the apposition ὄιές τε καὶ αἶγες 'sheep and goats' spells out which. ἰαύεσκον is an iterative imperfect of ἰαύω 'sleep, lie down for the night', with the ending -εσκον that marks a habit: they used to sleep there.

sentences.t:
περὶ δ’ αὐλὴ
ὑψηλὴ δέδμητο κατωρυχέεσσι λίθοισι
μακρῇσίν τε πίτυσσιν ἰδὲ δρυσὶν ὑψικόμοισιν.
sentences.tr:
peri d’ aulē
hypsēlē dedmēto katōrycheessi lithoisi
makrēisin te pityssin ide drysin hypsikomoisin.
sentences.l:
and around, a courtyard
high had been built with dug-in stones
and with tall pines and with high-crowned oaks.
sentences.i: and around it a high yard had been built, of stones sunk deep in the ground and of tall pines and high-crowned oaks.
sentences.n: περί is an adverb, 'around (it)', and αὐλή is 'courtyard, yard'. δέδμητο is a pluperfect passive of δέμω 'build', agreeing with αὐλή. The datives say what it was built of: κατωρυχέεσσι λίθοισι is 'stones dug down into the ground' (from κατορύσσω), stones set in the earth, and μακρῇσίν τε πίτυσσιν ἰδὲ δρυσὶν ὑψικόμοισιν is 'tall pines and high-crowned oaks', πίτυς 'pine' and δρῦς 'oak', with ἰδέ 'and'. ὑψικόμοισιν is 'high-haired' (κόμη 'hair, foliage'), that is with high leafy tops.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα δ’ ἀνὴρ ἐνίαυε πελώριος, ὅς ῥα τὰ μῆλα
οἶος ποιμαίνεσκεν ἀπόπροθεν·
sentences.tr:
entha d’ anēr eniaue pelōrios, hos rha ta mēla
oios poimainesken apoprothen·
sentences.l:
And there a man used to sleep, monstrous, who, those flocks,
alone was wont to shepherd, far off;
sentences.i: A monstrous man used to sleep there, who tended those flocks alone, far away;
sentences.n: ἀνήρ is 'man': the Cyclops is not yet named or called by the name of his people. πελώριος is 'monstrous, huge' and ἐνίαυε 'used to spend the night' (ἰαύω, as ἰαύεσκον at 184). ὅς ῥα is 'who', with the relative and the particle ῥα, and τὰ μῆλα is 'those flocks', with the article as a pronoun. ποιμαίνεσκεν is another iterative in -εσκον, 'used to shepherd'; οἶος is 'alone', and ἀπόπροθεν is 'from afar', with -θεν. What he is far from is stated in the next unit.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ μετ’ ἄλλους
πωλεῖτ’, ἀλλ’ ἀπάνευθεν ἐὼν ἀθεμίστια ᾔδη.
sentences.tr:
oude met’ allous
pōleit’, all’ apaneuthen eōn athemistia ēidē.
sentences.l:
nor among others
did he go about, but, being apart, lawless things he knew.
sentences.i: and he did not go about among others, but lived apart, versed in lawless ways.
sentences.n: πωλεῖτ’ is πωλεῖτο, 'used to go about, frequent', with μετ’ ἄλλους 'among others'. ἀπάνευθεν is 'apart, aloof', and ἐών is the epic participle of εἰμί (= ὤν). ἀθεμίστια is 'lawless things', from ἀθεμίστιος, of the same family as ἀθέμιστος at 106. ᾔδη is the past of οἶδα, 'he knew', and with an object of this kind it comes to mean 'was versed in, was minded to'.

sentences.t:
καὶ γὰρ θαῦμ’ ἐτέτυκτο πελώριον, οὐδὲ ἐῴκει
ἀνδρί γε σιτοφάγῳ, ἀλλὰ ῥίῳ ὑλήεντι
ὑψηλῶν ὀρέων, ὅ τε φαίνεται οἶον ἀπ’ ἄλλων.
sentences.tr:
kai gar thaum’ etetykto pelōrion, oude eōikei
andri ge sitophagōi, alla rhiōi hylēenti
hypsēlōn oreōn, ho te phainetai oion ap’ allōn.
sentences.l:
For indeed a marvel he had been made, monstrous, and he was not like
a grain-eating man, but like a wooded peak
of high mountains, which appears alone, apart from the others.
sentences.i: For he had been made a monstrous marvel, and not like a man who eats grain, but like a wooded peak of high mountains, which shows up alone, apart from the rest.
sentences.n: καὶ γὰρ is 'for indeed', and θαῦμ’ (θαῦμα) is 'marvel, wonder', with πελώριον. ἐτέτυκτο is a pluperfect passive of τεύχω 'make': 'he had been fashioned a marvel'. οὐδὲ ἐῴκει is 'nor was he like' (a pluperfect of ἔοικα, with the dative). ἀνδρὶ σιτοφάγῳ is 'a grain-eating man', σῖτος being the grain that ordinary men live on, and compare the crops that grow unsown in the Cyclopes' land, 109–111. ῥίῳ ὑλήεντι is 'a wooded peak', ῥίον being a peak or headland, and ὑλήεις 'wooded'. ὅ τε is 'which', with the epic τε for what is generally so; φαίνεται οἶον is 'shows alone', and ἀπ’ ἄλλων 'apart from the others', that is from other peaks. The speech goes on into the next part.
